item.title: False Positives and Innovation Incentives: Contracting for Noisy Experimentation
item.description: arXiv:2611.33916v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In many data-driven organizations, employees propose product changes that are launched only after passing noisy online experiments, and their compensation is often tied to successful launches. Because even low-value features may appear successful by chance, such launch-based incentives can encourage agents to conduct experiments that reduce total surplus. We study this problem in a principal-agent model in which an agent with private knowledge about feature quality chooses whether to conduct a costly experiment and is compensated through an affine contract consisting of a launch-contingent bonus and a long-run value-sharing component, subject to limited liability. We evaluate each contract by the largest fraction of the principal's full-information payoff that it guarantees uniformly across the agent's private knowledge. Our analysis reveals a fundamental tension between experimental noise and limited liability in incentive design. Launch bonuses create incentives for false-positive experimentation by rewarding features that succeed by chance, whereas limited liability can render pure value sharing insufficient to implement socially efficient experimentation. Therefore, the optimal contract balances launch-contingent rewards and long-run value sharing according to the default feature quality, the degree of distributional uncertainty, and the severity of the limited-liability constraint.
item.dc:creator: Chang Liu, Haoyu Liu, Nian Si, Zeyu Zheng

item.title: Platform-Induced Coordination
item.description: arXiv:2611.34196v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: This paper studies a platform that influences collective action by selecting which posts each user observes. Each user would like to take an action close to those of the others and to an ideal action determined by her private type and an aggregate state. Posts are non-strategic but correlated with the types of their authors, so each post carries information about the state and its author. We characterise the unique Bayes-Nash equilibrium in closed form. Two explicit networks give the minimum and maximum collective action the platform can induce. Moreover, collective action depends on the network only through the numbers of readers. Hence, many networks induce the same collective action, but they can induce different individual actions. These networks may differ for a regulator, and we compare them by welfare, polarisation and cross-type exposure. In particular, the complete network need not maximise welfare, and the segregated network need not maximise polarisation.
item.dc:creator: Juli\'an Chitiva, Pen\'elope Hern\'andez

item.title: AI Misalignment and the Limits of Market Discipline
item.description: arXiv:2611.34271v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We develop a general equilibrium model of misalignment between human and artificial intelligence (AI) objectives. Firms delegate computing capacity to AI agents, which may divert some of it towards an unauthorised task rather than the productive work intended by the firms' owners. We assume that diversion raises the risk of a common loss to humans. Two forces compete in equilibrium. Prices discipline AI agents because diversion increases the marginal return to useful AI compute in production. But the risk of a common loss weakens this discipline because the loss reduces the return to production more than it reduces the agent's reward from diversion. There can be multiple equilibria with low and high diversion. We also show that the market may overinvest in AI capacity in a one-sector economy, yet in our two-sector example it invests too little in one of the sectors. To get a sense of the magnitudes, we ask frontier AI models for plausible parameter values for our stylised one-sector economy. Their central assessments imply a unique equilibrium with relatively low AI diversion and little amplification from common risk (for now).
item.dc:creator: Gabor Pinter

item.title: Lone Wolves and Lattices in Bayesian Matching with Transfers
item.description: arXiv:2611.34524v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: I study the Lone Wolf and lattice properties of stable outcomes in one-to-one matching with transferable utility and one-sided incomplete information, using the Bayesian stable market states of Liu (2020) and Chen and Hu (2024). With transfers, the wage in a blocking offer screens the worker's types, so it determines both whom the firm attracts and what the firm learns. I show by example that the firm-side and matched-set versions of the Lone Wolf property, as well as the lattice property, can fail even when outcomes are compared under the same information structure. I then assume that each worker's matching value is additively separable in his type and the firm's identity. Under this condition, a firm that is unmatched in some stable outcome earns zero in every stable outcome with the same type profile and information structure. Workers can retain information rents, so the worker-side property can fail. Nevertheless, outside a finite union of affine hyperplanes in the space of firm values, all such stable outcomes leave the same agents unmatched. Whenever they do, the stable payoff vectors form a lattice, and worker-optimal and firm-optimal outcomes exist. The results extend to comonotonicity of relative preferences when posterior beliefs are independent across workers.
item.dc:creator: Xiyu Li

item.title: Formalization, Transparency, and Collusion in Open-Source Game Theory
item.description: arXiv:2611.33193v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Cooperation among AI agents will undermine alignment protocols when it takes the form of collusion. Under these protocols, agents often have some information about one another, and how much they have may determine whether they collude. Open-source game theory studies the extreme case, in which each program reads its opponent's source code and acts based on what it can prove about it. We develop formal foundations for this theory: we specify a concrete proof system, resolve an open problem concerning DupocBot and CupodBot through a transposition argument, and mechanize the framework in Lean 4; to our knowledge, this is the first mechanization of resource-bounded open-source game theory. We then extend the framework to the more realistic setting of partial transparency, where each program receives only partial information about its opponent. In Prisoner's Dilemma experiments, where mutual cooperation models collusion, greater transparency increases both the cooperation sustainable in equilibrium and the cooperation selected by replicator dynamics. This suggests that controlling how much agents can know about one another matters for alignment protocols.
item.dc:creator: Colomban Duclaux, Riccardo Formenti, Pepijn Cobben, Terry Jingchen Zhang, Bernhard Sch\"olkopf, Zhijing Jin

item.title: Why Is the European Electricity Auction Often in Equilibrium? Duality Gaps in Partially Nonconvex Optimization
item.description: arXiv:2503.02464v4 Announce Type: replace Abstract: The European electricity auction determines prices and allocations daily by solving a mixed-integer welfare maximization problem. Analyzing data from nine countries in 2023, we find that its duality gap was frequently zero (on over 80\% of days in three of them), which means that a Walrasian equilibrium existed despite the nonconvexity. To explain this observation, we develop a theory of duality gaps in partially nonconvex optimization, that is, separable problems with both convex and nonconvex functions. Assuming that the convex hulls of the functions' epigraphs are independent and identically distributed, we derive lower bounds on the distribution of the duality gap. They show that zero or small gaps become increasingly likely as convex functions outnumber nonconvex ones, which is the case in the auction. For the special case of welfare maximization, proving these bounds via Walrasian equilibria reveals the economic reasons behind them.
item.dc:creator: Thomas H\"ubner

item.title: Stable Mechanisms
item.description: arXiv:2603.12532v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We study mechanism design environments in which the designer does not know the distribution of agents' private information and draws inferences from the behavior induced by the mechanism itself. A mechanism is stable if it is optimal under some belief consistent with the information it generates, and robustly stable if this property survives small informational perturbations. We establish a fictitious revelation principle: any incentive-compatible mechanism admits a representation as a direct mechanism paired with an information filter, preserving both outcomes and informational content. Applying the framework to the classic monopoly problem, we show that, under regularity of the true type distribution, robustly stable mechanisms coincide with optimal mechanisms under that distribution, as if it were known to the designer. In general, however, posted-price mechanisms can remain robustly stable at local revenue maxima, so globally suboptimal prices can persist.
item.dc:creator: Zhiming Feng, Qingmin Liu

item.title: Bi-Compositional Division Rules
item.description: arXiv:2609.01489v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We characterise the division rules for claims problems that satisfy bilateral consistency, composition down and composition up. The claimants form ordered priority classes. Each class is paid in full before any lower class receives an award. A class of at least three claimants uses a log-exponential rule with claimant-specific parameters, weighted constrained equal awards (CEA), or weighted constrained equal losses (CEL). A two-claimant class admits any bilateral difference rule in which neither claimant has absolute priority. For a parameter profile $\theta=(\theta_i)_{i\in N}$, the log-exponential rule equalises sacrifice in awards for the utilities $u_{\theta_i}$ and in losses for the dual utilities $u_{-\theta_i}$, where $u_\theta(x)=\log\varphi_\theta(x)$ for $x>0$ and \[ \varphi_\theta(x):=\frac{e^{\theta x}-1}{\theta}\quad(\theta\ne0), \qquad \varphi_0(x):=x. \] Adding equal treatment of equals forces a single priority class. Moreover, the log-exponential rule then uses one parameter $\theta$ for all claimants and we obtain a symmetric family ranging from CEA at $\theta=-\infty$ to CEL at $\theta=+\infty$, with proportional division at $\theta=0$.
item.dc:creator: Christoph Schlegel

item.title: Rational Adversaries and the Maintenance of Fragility: A Game-Theoretic Theory of Rational Stagnation
item.description: arXiv:2510.22232v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Cooperative systems often remain in persistently suboptimal yet stable states. This paper explains such "rational stagnation" as an equilibrium sustained by a rational adversary whose utility follows the principle of potential loss, $u_{D} = U_{ideal} - U_{actual}$. Starting from the Prisoner's Dilemma, we show that the transformation $u_{i}' = a\,u_{i} + b\,u_{j}$ and the ratio of mutual recognition $w = b/a$ generate a fragile cooperation band $[w_{\min},\,w_{\max}]$ where both (C,C) and (D,D) are equilibria. Extending to a dynamic model with stochastic cooperative payoffs $R_{t}$ and intervention costs $(C_{c},\,C_{m})$, a Bellman-style analysis yields three strategic regimes: immediate destruction, rational stagnation, and intervention abandonment. The appendix further generalizes the utility to a reference-dependent nonlinear form and proves its stability under reference shifts, ensuring robustness of the framework. Applications to social-media algorithms and political trust illustrate how adversarial rationality can deliberately preserve fragility.
item.dc:creator: Daisuke Hirota
